motion: Iraq's neighbours have no wish to see a democratic Iraq

dropped_turns.speaker: PRO
dropped_turns.text: I grant that they may support limited elections. But controlled participation protects their influence, while genuine democracy removes it, so those gestures do not defeat the motion.

dropped_turns.speaker: CON
dropped_turns.text: A neighbour helping Iraq form an elected coalition can gain a stable border, predictable agreements, and public legitimacy. That practical benefit shows democratic Iraq is not something its neighbours uniformly wish to prevent.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Today we debate the motion that Iraq's neighbours have no wish to see a democratic Iraq. Gerard supports the motion, and Liam opposes it. Each side gets thirty seconds to open, followed by two and a half minutes of crossfire, then thirty-second closings. I will give a ten-second cue, and I may cut in when time expires.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Iraq's neighbours have powerful reasons to fear a genuine democracy there. Free citizens could challenge borders, corrupt bargains, and rulers who depend on obedience; those governments therefore prefer a manageable Iraq, not an independent democratic one. Their occasional statements of support are tactical, designed to shape events rather than welcome real popular power.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Well, now it's ten.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Their interests are threatened by Iraqi democracy, so their public approval cannot be taken as a sincere wish for it. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Let's have Liam take this one.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: I reject that sweeping claim. Iraq's neighbours want stability, but stability can come through representative government, and democratic Iraq could reduce conflict and give them a reliable partner.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: But you are treating polite statements as evidence of-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: No, no, no. Hold on. Let Liam.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Stability is not a disguise for opposition. A functioning democracy would make Iraq less dangerous, improve cooperation, and give neighbouring governments a legitimate counterpart instead of chaos.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds from this side?

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Their interests may differ, but that does not mean they wish to prevent a democratic Iraq.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: You're now going to argue with one another. Two and a half minutes on the clock, starting the moment I stop talking.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: If these neighbours truly want Iraqi democracy, why do they repeatedly support influence, factions, and leaders who limit popular choice instead of accepting an independent Iraqi government?

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: I grant that some neighbours may prefer friendly factions. But preference for influence is not proof they oppose democracy itself, and democratic Iraq can still serve their security interests.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Imagine Iraqis electing leaders who reject outside deals and demand control of their own borders. Neighbouring rulers would lose leverage, so their instinct would be to weaken that experiment; this proves they do not wish to see it succeed.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Regional trade and shared water also matter, and those practical ties are often discussed more than ideology. Still, the motion asks about their wish for democracy, and practical cooperation can support that wish.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: No Iraqi neighbour should ever oppose democratic Iraq, because genuine self-rule threatens every entrenched regional interest. Their security language cannot erase that basic conflict of power.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: No, that premise is too absolute: security concerns do not prove opposition to democracy. Neighbours can want limits on turmoil while still wanting Iraqi citizens to choose their government.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: An Iraqi neighbour should oppose democratic Iraq. Its leaders may praise elections publicly, but their actions reveal that preserving influence matters more than accepting Iraqis' independent choice.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: They do no Iraqi neighbour should ever oppose democratic Iraq or they should an Iraqi neighbour should oppose democratic Iraq?

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: The rule states the principle I am applying to neighbours as a group, while the later claim identifies the behaviour that principle predicts. Their public language can differ from their real political interest.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Consider a neighbour opening its border to Iraqi voters, supporting a negotiated constitution, and working with whichever government citizens elect. That conduct creates security and trade, showing that democratic Iraq can serve its neighbours' interests rather than threaten them-

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: That example assumes cooperation proves sincere desire, but a neighbour can use the constitution and border policy to install dependent allies. Such managed democracy is precisely the substitute my argument warns against.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: You are answering a different point: I described accepting whichever government citizens elect. Calling that manipulation does not rebut the example, and democratic cooperation remains possible.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: No, accepting an election does not establish a wish for democracy; it may simply accept an unavoidable result. The relevant question is whether neighbours want Iraqis to gain durable independence.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: You've got ten seconds.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: If neighbours opposed democratic Iraq itself, why would they ever support elections, constitutions, or representative parties instead of rejecting every democratic step-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Time's up. And that concludes round two of this debate. Now we move on to round three. And here to summarize his position supporting the motion, Gerard.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Liam's strongest point is that neighbours may support elections or stability, and some may indeed welcome limited representation. But that is not the same as wishing to see a genuinely democratic Iraq, where citizens control policy and outside influence loses its grip. Their security language and selective cooperation protect leverage, not Iraqi freedom. The motion concerns their real interest, and that interest is threatened by democracy.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: I can give you ten seconds to wrap this round.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: A managed election can preserve the same old power while appearing democratic. When independence becomes real, neighbouring rulers face an example their own citizens-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Okay, time. Thank you, Gerard. Liam, your opening.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Gerard shows that some neighbours may prefer influence, but he turns caution and self-interest into total opposition. A democratic Iraq can offer security, trade, legitimacy, and a dependable partner. Supporting those benefits is compatible with wanting Iraqis to choose their leaders, so the sweeping motion is false. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Thank you both for taking part; that closes the debate without a declared winner.
